section: Child Development & Pedagogy · Ch1 — Development: Principles
subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: An infant gains control of the head and trunk before the arms and legs. This illustrates which principle of development?
explanation: Cephalocaudal ('head-to-tail') development proceeds from head downward. The proximodistal principle is centre-outward (trunk before fingers). Both are directional growth principles.

section: Child Development & Pedagogy · Ch1 — Development: Principles
subject: Child Development & Pedagogy

options.option_text: Growth is quantitative and measurable; development is qualitative and continuous throughout life
Growth continues lifelong; development stops at adolescence
Growth is qualitative; development is only physical
Growth and development are exact synonyms in psychology

explanation: Growth denotes measurable increase in size/weight and generally ceases at maturity; development is qualitative, progressive and lifelong, involving change in structure and function.

section: Child Development & Pedagogy · Ch1 — Development: Principles
subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: The contemporary consensus on the 'nature versus nurture' debate in child development is that:

options.option_text: Heredity and environment interact continuously to shape development
Heredity alone fully determines all abilities
Environment alone fully determines all abilities
Neither heredity nor environment has any measurable effect

explanation: Development is the product of ongoing interaction between genetic endowment (nature) and experience/environment (nurture); neither operates alone.

section: Child Development & Pedagogy · Ch1 — Development: Principles
subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: A teacher notices a child is physically strong but struggles to share and cooperate with peers. The child is comparatively weaker in which domain of development?
explanation: Sharing, cooperation and managing relationships fall under the social-emotional domain. Development across physical, cognitive, language and social-emotional domains can proceed at different rates in the same child.

section: Child Development & Pedagogy · Ch1 — Development: Principles
subject: Child Development & Pedagogy
stem: The primary agency of socialisation for a young child, before school, is the:
explanation: The family is the first and primary agency of socialisation, shaping language, values and habits before secondary agencies (school, peers, media) take a larger role.
